courseDescriptionInputs.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

Students study AI's capabilities and limits, applications across business functions and industries, and effects on labour markets, productivity, innovation and inequality. Business cases and scholarly arguments support analysis of governance, regulation and a country's AI readiness and industrial policy.

courseDescriptionInputs.text: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.

courseDescriptionInputs.text: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.

readerValues.programmeDescription: Economics & Society at Leiden combines economic theory and empirical analysis with law, politics and institutions. Students examine welfare, inequality, climate change, migration and labour markets, and learn to assess economic policy and its social consequences. The programme is taught in The Hague in cooperation with Erasmus School of Economics. Tutoring supports academic and career development.
readerValues.comparisonExplanation: This qualified academic-core comparison assesses the confirmed first 120 EC with Package A. Three UCR programs combine economic theory and empirical analysis with institutions, behavior and inequality, or climate governance. All 180 EC of the published outline remain visible, but the final 30 required EC and project are shown only at outline level and are outside the academic comparison. Dutch fiscal/social law, specialist labour/migration study, integrated climate-economic modelling and some causal methods remain differences.

curriculum.limitation: The published outline totals 180 EC, including 30 EC of elective space and a 10-EC bachelor project. Detailed third-year, cohort and project requirements remain unconfirmed. This is an indicative programme outline, not a certified complete degree pathway.
